rows.question: Can the Route10 power both of its PoE+ ports at the full 30 W per port at the same time?
rows.expected: No: 2 ports x 30 W = 60 W, but the Route10 PoE budget is 40 W
rows.answer: No: the Route10 has two PoE+ ports (ports 2 and 3, 802.3at) but a total PoE budget of only 40W. [1][2] Powering both ports at 30 W each would require 30 W + 30 W = 60 W, which exceeds the 40W budget by 20 W. [2] Each port is rated at 54VDC, 0.6A max, which is 54 V × 0.6 A = 32.4 W per port, so a single port can deliver full PoE+ power but both together are capped by the 40W total budget. [2]

rows.question: Both fall detection papers use an ESP32. How does each one send its sensor data?
rows.expected: Adebesin et al.: the ESP32 sends over LoRa to a gateway; bathroom study: ESP32-C3 nodes send 2.56 s windows over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi 4B
rows.answer: In the Adebesin et al. wearable fall detection system, a Freenove ESP32-WROVER CAM board transmits acceleration and velocity readings over LoRa using an RYLR896 UART LoRa transceiver module (868/915MHz) to an application that processes the data for training and prediction. [1] An Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) mechanism ensures reliable transmission of these readouts through retransmissions. [2] In the bathroom fall detection paper (arXiv 2603.17069), the ESP32-C3 nodes performed sensing, timestamping and lightweight preprocessing, then transmitted buffered 2.56 s windows over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi 4B edge gateway. [3] Both of its ESP32-C3 sensing nodes (ADXL345 vibration and C4001 mmWave radar) shared ESP32-based time synchronization. [4]
removed: numbers not in the quote: 4 :: Sensor data is sent from the wearable to a gateway via LoRa, using 6LoWPAN/IPv6, UDP and CoAP, then forwarded to the cloud over Ethernet with IPv4, TCP and HTTP

rows.question: What sampling rate does each fall detection paper use for its sensor data?
rows.expected: Adebesin et al.: 20 Hz (50 ms); bathroom study: streams mapped to a common 100 Hz
rows.answer: In adebesin2026 (wearable fall detection with LoRa), sensors were sampled at a fixed rate of 20 Hz (50 ms per sample) for fall-detection experiments, and both the IMU fall detection and piezoelectric sensor datasets are listed at 20 Hz. [1][3] For baseline activities in adebesin2026, the sampling period was dynamic, ranging from 500 ms to 50 ms. [2] In the bathroom fall detection paper (arXiv 2603.17069), the mmWave radar node produced 3D point clouds at 12.5 Hz, while the vibration node sampled at 200 Hz and was resampled to 100 Hz. [4][5] That paper maps the radar and vibration streams to a common 100 Hz rate and slices them into 2.56 s windows of 256 samples with 50% overlap. [6]

rows.question: On the Raspberry Pi 4B, how does the end-to-end latency of the radar-only model compare with the radar and vibration fusion model in the bathroom study?
rows.expected: Radar only 28.4 ms vs fusion 15.8 ms
rows.answer: In the bathroom fall detection paper (arXiv 2603.17069), the Motion-Mamba radar-only model on the Raspberry Pi 4B has an end-to-end latency of 28.4 ms (7.5 ms preprocessing, 19.8 ms inference). [1] The full radar and vibration fusion model achieves 15.8 ms end-to-end latency on the Raspberry Pi 4B (8.9 ms preprocessing, 6.7 ms inference). [2] The fusion model is therefore 28.4 ms - 15.8 ms = 12.6 ms faster end-to-end than the radar-only model, about 1.8x lower latency (28.4 / 15.8 ≈ 1.80). [1][2] The fusion model's preprocessing is 1.4 ms longer (8.9 ms vs 7.5 ms), but its inference is 13.1 ms shorter (6.7 ms vs 19.8 ms), and that more than offsets the extra preprocessing. [1][2]
removed: numbers not in the quote: 35.9 :: The fusion model achieves 15.8 ms latency and 10750 mJ per window on the Raspberry Pi 4B, compared with 35.9 ms for the strongest baseline.
